title: Rehat at work
hookLine: keeping the articles of faith in workplaces far from Punjab

lines: A NURSE, A COOK, A FOREMAN.
AN ORDINARY SHIFT, WITH THE REHAT ALONG.
cards: Five forty-five in the morning, a hospital locker room. A nurse finishes Japji on her phone with one earbud in, ties her hair under a surgical cap, slides her kara up her forearm and tapes it for the shift.
Across town a cook pulls a net over his beard before the first ticket prints. On a building site, a foreman raises, once again, the question of a hard hat over his turban. None of them are in Punjab.
After the kirpan and the law, something smaller and more daily: an ordinary shift.

teach.h: ANG 1245: EARN, AND GIVE SOME AWAY.
teach.b: Start with the job itself, which in Sikh teaching is part of the path.

teach.h: KIRAT: HONEST WORK IS PART OF THE PATH.
teach.b: Early on, you met kirat, honest work, and the line earn it clean.
Guru Nanak puts it in one line on Ang 1245, in paraphrase: the one who eats what they earn by their own effort, and gives some of it away, has recognized the way.
Earning isn't a break from the spiritual life; it sits right beside giving. So a Sikh at work isn't stepping out of the rehat for the length of a shift. The workplace is one more place it gets kept.

teach.h: THE ARTICLES GO TO WORK TOO.
teach.b: The articles of faith go to work too. The kesh stays uncut and covered, under a turban, a patka, a cap, a net. The kara stays on the wrist.
The kirpan is worn in whatever way the place and its laws allow.
That often takes conversations, with a manager, a safety officer, a uniform supplier, and Sikhs in different countries have had them one workplace at a time, with answers that vary.
And there's a third side, which belongs to everyone else. A colleague's turban, beard or kara isn't a costume or a quirk.

teach.h: A PROMISE, KEPT ON COMPANY TIME.
teach.b: It's a promise, kept on company time. Respect at work can be as simple as asking a real question once, and then letting it be normal.

how: Sikhs who keep the articles of faith wear them at work, adapting to safety rules and uniforms (a patka or net over the kesh, a kara taped for a shift), and Sikh teaching counts honest earning, kirat, as part of the path.

practice: Bring to mind someone you work or study with whose faith, diet, prayer times or clothing differ from yours, and picture them going through their day, keeping something that matters to them.
Notice whether you've ever made that harder, even with a joke or a sigh. Then picture one small way to make it easier: a meeting time, a lunch order, a plain question asked kindly.

wordCard.voice: Rehat at work. For Sikhs, honest work is part of the path, and the articles of faith go to the job too, worked out with each workplace. Today's word.
